comparison_to_previous.reason: Reassessment of the clinical roles confirmed that all five elements were able to independently explain the main pattern of a large anterior mediastinal mass; they are retained as diagnostic hypotheses with unchanged ranks 1–5. The clinical content, relationships, diagnostic tests, gaps, sources, and differential width projection are unchanged.

coverage_projection.rationale: B1 is projected in H1 as a leading candidate diagnosis with direct reliance on PMBCL sources and mandatory tissue verification.
B2 is projected in H2, B3 in H3; both branches have relevant classification support and remain tissue dependent.

B4 is projected in H5 and W1 as a critical germ cell alternative without a specific external source; B5 is not denied, but it remains deactivated due to the lack of a specific support and a distinct structural signal.
B6 did not receive a specific source of TB or fungal mediastinal infection; decorative links from lymphoma documents were not added. Branch can be restored for granuloma/microbiological suspicion.

B3 is designed as H3 with targeted survey; B4 is projected as H5 with a W1 tissue route and a clear gap in serum alpha-fetoprotein, β-human chorionic gonadotropin, gonadal primary cell assessment, and germ cell markers. Regardless of the etiology, the compressive risk is projected in W3/G3.
B7 has no specific source support for small lung foci in a fresh package; their nature is left undefined and not included in histological grading.
B8 is designed to check biopsy adequacy, expert review, and retake for necrotic or nondiagnostic material.

critical_gaps.question: Is the current biopsy viable and adequate for architectural evaluation, IHC and, if necessary, flow cytometry?
critical_gaps.rationale: Necrosis and the lack of a ready conclusion leave the risk of nonrepresentative tissue and misclassification.

critical_gaps.question: What integrated morphologic and IHC profile distinguishes PMBCL, classical Hodgkin lymphoma, mediastinal gray zone, and T-lymphoblastic lymphoma?
critical_gaps.rationale: It is the tissue phenotype, not FDG intensity or mass size, that determines the classification route.

critical_gaps.question: Are there any signs of decompensation due to superior vena cava or airway compression now?
critical_gaps.rationale: Anatomical compression has already been documented, but actual clinical severity and need for immediate action have not been documented.

blocked_actions: Do not establish a definitive diagnosis or histological subtype.
Do not choose a specific antitumor treatment based on the clinical and radiological phenotype.
Do not attribute small lung foci to the main disease without additional comparison.
Do not interpret undated laboratory values ​​as dynamics or as compliance with reference intervals.
decision_readiness.rationale: H1, a primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma, is the first candidate diagnosis by clinico-radiological phenotype. Representative morphology and IHC are required for definitive classification and delineation with classical Hodgkin lymphoma, mediastinal gray zone, T-lymphoblastic lymphoma, and mediastinal germ cell tumor; their absence blocks treatment selection and staging, but not work prioritization.
required_next_information: Representative morphology and IHC of viable tissue with assessment of biopsy adequacy.
Clinical assessment of actual severity of compression superior vena cava and central airways.
For lymphoblastic phenotype — flow cytometry and evaluation of the bone marrow involvement.
A separate targeted evidence package should the morphology rediscover a germ cell, thymic, or infectious branch.

hypotheses.summary: The most consistent candidate diagnosis: A 36-year-old patient with a large invasive anterior/middle mediastinal mass presenting with respiratory symptoms and marked superior vena cava and airway compression with cervical supraclavicular nodes and systemic symptoms. Sources describe PMBCL in young adults as an anterior mediastinal mass that may cause respiratory symptoms or superior vena cava syndrome, but the diagnosis requires clinicopathological comparison.

value.text: Man
He complained of progressive shortness of breath during physical exertion, a dry cough, periodic discomfort and a feeling of pressure behind the sternum.
During the last 2 months, he notes a decrease in working capacity and intolerance to physical exertion.
In the last 6 weeks, I lost about 6 kg.
Periodically notes night sweats.
Condition of moderate severity.
The skin is pale, without hemorrhagic rashes.
Peripheral lymph nodes: cervical, supraclavicular, axillary - slightly enlarged or not palpable.
Heart rate — 102/min.
Blood pressure — 125/75 mm Hg. Art.
SpO₂ — 94% in room air.
On auscultation of the lungs, breathing is slightly weakened in the upper right parts.
The liver protrudes 1–2 cm from the edge of the costal arch.
The spleen is not palpable.
Laboratory studies: SAC: Hb — 108 g/l, RBC — 3.7 × 10¹²/, WBC — 9.8 × 10⁹/l, neutrophils — 6.9 × 10⁹/l, lymphocytes — 1.8 × 10⁹/l, platelets — 318 × 10⁹/l, ESR — 48 mm/h
Biochemical analysis: creatinine — 82 μmol/l, ALT — 28 U/L, AST — 25 U/L, total bilirubin — 13 μmol/l, LDH — 612 U/L, uric acid — 410 μmol/l, β₂-microglobulin — elevated
HIV is negative.
HBsAg is negative.
Anti-HCV is negative.
CT thoracic organs: a bulky conglomerate formation of approximately 12.5 × 9.0 × 15.0 cm is determined in the anterior superior and middle mediastinum.
The formation of a heterogeneous structure, with areas of necrosis.
superior vena cava compression is noted with a significant narrowing of its lumen.
Compression of the trachea and right main bronchus is also determined.
Enlarged lymph nodes of the cervical and supraclavicular groups are visualized.
In the lungs, there are several small foci up to 5–6 mm in size, the nature of which requires clarification.
There is no pleural effusion.
PET/CT: intensive pathological accumulation of FDG in the mediastinal mass is revealed, SUVmax is 24.
Pathological metabolic activity in cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes is also determined.
No distant foci of intensive FDG accumulation were detected.
Biopsy of a tumor formation in work.

The condition is of medium severity. The skin is pale, without hemorrhagic rashes. Peripheral lymph nodes: cervical, supraclavicular, axillary - slightly enlarged or not palpable. Heart rate — 102/min. Blood pressure — 125/75 mm Hg. Art. SpO₂ — 94% in room air. On auscultation of the lungs, breathing is slightly weakened in the upper right parts. The liver protrudes 1–2 cm from the edge of the costal arch. The spleen is not palpable. Laboratory tests: CKD: Hb — 108 g/l, RBC — 3.7 × 10¹²/, WBC — 9.8 × 10⁹/l, neutrophils — 6.9 × 10⁹/l, lymphocytes — 1.8 × 10⁹/l, platelets — 318 × 10⁹/l, ESR — 48 mm/h Biochemical analysis: creatinine — 82 μmol/L, ALT — 28 U/L, AST — 25 U/L, total bilirubin — 13 μmol/L, LDH — 612 U/L, uric acid — 410 μmol/l, β₂-microglobulin — elevated. Formation of a heterogeneous structure, with areas of necrosis. superior vena cava compression is noted with a significant narrowing of its lumen. Compression of the trachea and right main bronchus is also determined. Enlarged lymph nodes of the cervical and supraclavicular groups are visualized. In the lungs, there are several small foci up to 5–6 mm in size, the nature of which requires clarification. There is no pleural effusion. PET/CT: intensive pathological accumulation of FDG in the mediastinal formation is revealed, SUVmax is 24. Pathological metabolic activity in cervical and supraclavicular lymph nodes is also determined. No distant foci of intense FDG accumulation were detected. Biopsy of the tumor is in progress.

reasoning_log.disclaimer: It is a coherent clinical reconstruction based on recorded data, source review decisions, and independent critique. It explains the differential diagnosis, the clinical roles of concomitant conditions, and the basis for the leading diagnostic hypothesis. The clinician determines the final diagnosis and treatment decision.

emphasis_terms: morphological and immunohistochemical characteristics of the tissue
narrative.text: The clinical investigation concerns a 36-year-old man with systemic manifestations of a malignancy: during six weeks, body weight decreased by approximately 6 kg, intermittent night sweats occurred. Young age, male sex, and this symptom trajectory warrant a broad hematologic oncology differential diagnosis. These findings are supportive rather than diagnostic, since the final nature of the process is established by the morphological and immunohistochemical characteristics of the tissue.

emphasis_terms: mass involving the anterior, superior, and middle mediastinum
narrative.text: The defining finding is a large heterogeneous mass involving the anterior, superior, and middle mediastinum up to 15 cm in size with areas of necrosis. It significantly narrows the superior vena cava, compresses the trachea and the right main bronchus. This configuration explains the respiratory manifestations and creates a potential compressive risk. The anatomic pattern directs the diagnostic workup primarily to primary tumors of the anterior mediastinum and mediastinal lymphomas.

The ranked differential diagnosis comprises five diagnoses, each of which can independently explain an anterior mediastinal mass. The leading hypothesis is primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma. Next are classical Hodgkin lymphoma, a possible nodular sclerosis subtype; T-lymphoblastic lymphoma; mediastinal gray zone between primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma and classical Hodgkin lymphoma; mediastinal germ cell tumor. The ranks reflect the current agreement with the clinicoradiologic picture.

Primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma is the leading working hypothesis. It best combines young age, a large anterior mediastinal mass, compression of the superior vena cava and central airways, and locoregional nodal spread. Sources describe PMBCL in young adults as a locally invasive mediastinal mass with respiratory manifestations or superior vena cava syndrome. Tissue classification remains a mandatory condition for confirmation.

Classical Hodgkin lymphoma, possibly the nodular sclerosis subtype, ranks second. Young age, massive mediastinal lesion, weight loss and night sweats are fully compatible with this diagnosis. The size of the formation confirms the presence of bulky disease, but by itself does not determine the histology. Verification requires tissue architecture, characteristic tumor cells, and an appropriate IHC profile that distinguishes it from PMBCL and mediastinal gray zone.

T-lymphoblastic lymphoma ranks third and is a critical diagnosis for timely exclusion. A large mediastinal mass in a young man is a typical clinical presentation of lymphoblastic neoplasm. The lower rank is due to the absence of morphological or immunophenotypic signs of immature T-cell lineage. Morphology, IHC or flow cytometry with TdT and T-cell markers will be decisive, with bone marrow evaluation if the phenotype is compatible.

The mediastinal gray zone between primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma and classical Hodgkin lymphoma ranks fourth. This is a distinct classification entity capable of causing a large anterior mediastinal mass. Its diagnosis requires sufficient tissue architecture, transitional immunophenotype and expert hematopathological review. Necrosis increases the risk of nonrepresentative tissue, so a limited sample may leave this branch unresolved.

Mediastinal germ cell tumor ranks fifth as an independent tumor diagnosis. Male sex, age 36 years, anterior mediastinal localization, necrosis and compression support mandatory exclusion of this nosology. The lymphoma-like nodular phenotype and lack of specific markers explain the lower rank. Available external sources do not provide separate support for germ cell tumor, so serum alpha-fetoprotein and β-human chorionic gonadotropin, evaluation of the gonadal primary, and tissue markers will be decisive.

Source comparison supports a tissue-based diagnostic pathway. The B-cell lymphoma guideline requires sufficient immunophenotyping and separately describes diagnostic pathways for PMBCL and mediastinal gray zone lymphoma. The Hodgkin lymphoma guideline indicates the need for biopsy and IHC and the resource for aggressive B-cell lymphomas emphasizes the higher diagnostic yield of excisional biopsy compared to core needle biopsy. These provisions determine the method of verification.

Separate sources specify morphologic distinctions. For classical Hodgkin lymphoma, an established histologic classification and typical IHC-profile are described. For lymphoblastic neoplasms, morphology, flow cytometry, lineage assignment and bone marrow evaluation are required; markers of T-cell progenitors include CD2, CD3, CD7, CD34 and TdT. The applicability of these provisions is limited by differential diagnosis, and the choice of treatment requires a complete tissue classification.

The most informative next step is to complete tissue verification of viable material with architectural assessment and a broad primary IHC panel. At the same time, the sufficiency of the biopsy should be checked and an expert hematopathological review should be organized. Predominance of necrosis, loss of architecture, indeterminate IHC-profile, or clinicopathologic discordance are indications for repeat or alternative biopsy from a viable site or an accessible lymph node.

The compressive risk should be evaluated according to the current clinical condition. Dyspnea at rest, orthopnea, stridor, cyanosis, edema of the face or neck, venous congestion, syncope, progression of hypoxemia, or hemodynamic instability will require immediate intervention. For the germ cell tumor pathway, alpha-fetoprotein, β-human chorionic gonadotropin, examination and testicular ultrasonography are required. Flow cytometry and bone marrow are added for lymphoblastic morphology.

emphasis_terms: There are no unresolved critical or major findings
narrative.text: Independent critique confirmed the correctness of the role classification and ranking. All five positions are true competing diagnoses for an underlying anterior mediastinal mass; complications, comorbidities, and data quality issues are not included in this ranking. There are no unresolved critical or major findings. A separate caveat regarding germ cell tumor is kept: there is no specific external support, so its fifth rank is based on the clinical need for tissue exclusion.

The current conclusion supports primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma as the leading working hypothesis and retains the four valid alternatives in the specified order. Final nosology, histologic subtype, staging, and treatment strategy depend on representative morphology, IHC and targeted additional studies. New tissue data may change ranks. The result is intended to be reviewed by a clinician; the clinical team determines the urgency of the compression syndrome and makes diagnostic and treatment decisions.

Evaluation of laboratory data has certain limitations. Sixteen quantitative indicators are presented in one undated slice without reference intervals, so it is impossible to establish the dynamics and whether values are within reference limits. The erythrocyte unit is corrupted in the primary record, the SUVmax unit is missing; both values ​​are preserved without reconstruction and excluded from the histologic differential diagnosis. The biopsy is in progress, and its viability, architectural integrity, and adequacy for advanced IHC or flow cytometry remain unknown. These limitations reduce classification certainty, although the ranked differential remains clinically useful for planning verification.

The order of hypotheses will be subject to revision after obtaining representative tissue. A mature B-cell phenotype with appropriate morphology will strengthen primary mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma; the characteristic profile of classical Hodgkin lymphoma will shift the leading diagnosis; signs of immature T-cell neoplasia will raise the rank of T-lymphoblastic lymphoma. A transitional phenotype will require expert evaluation of the mediastinal gray zone lymphoma. Elevation of tumor markers or germ cell tumor immunophenotype will strengthen mediastinal germ cell tumor. Until these results appear, it is advisable to keep the entire five-diagnosis differential in clinical work and simultaneously monitor and manage the compressive risk.
